fullText:
Great paper from Google on making ML experiments reproducible for coding agents.

(bookmark it)

If you run agents on research code, this one is worth your time.

They find that refined artifacts raise agent reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% across four models and cut API spending by 19.7%.

ReproBridge turns one successful reproduction into a package the next agent can reuse. The package holds the cleaned code, the environment setup, scripts that launch each experiment, and a written guide.

A new agent reruns the experiment from that package. A separate auditor then checks that the runs actually happened.

The benchmark covers 1,029 tasks from 36 papers, each with five human-verified reference scores. The gap between the best and worst model drops from 21.6 to 3.9 points. Removing the code or the environment setup causes the largest losses.

If your agents keep failing to rerun a repo, save the setup steps from the first successful run before trying a bigger model.

https://t.co/sKYl7Nf77S

fullText:
Great paper finds that MCP agents rarely say that tasks are impossible.

They propose MCPHallu, which runs 358 tasks on 36 production MCP servers.

Each task is built to trigger one failure type, such as branch collapse, an unreachable goal, tool misuse, or forgetting context.

Across fourteen frontier agents and 5,012 trajectories, the average score is 0.642 out of 1.

On unreachable-goal tasks, only 23.2% of runs pass. Agents keep calling tools or report success instead of saying the goal cannot be met.

A model's rank moves by 6.9 of 13 places on average depending on the failure type.

The main takeaway is that you want to pick models for MCP work by the failure type your users hit most, and add tests where the right answer is to stop.

user.name: Michael Black
user.description: VP Digital Human Research, Epic Games. Emeritus Director, Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems (@MPI_IS). Opinions are my own.

fullText:
Writing software for human use is different from writing software for an AI.

For humans, we provide an API/CLI/GUI that defines a contract. It controls what the valid inputs are and how the software should respond. The software itself is immutable.

We do this because we don't expect users of software to be able to easily modify it. We don’t expect everyone to be an expert and very fast programmer. We also do this because a contract is useful – it defines what the creator of the software commits to and what they don’t.

The future is that we write software for AIs to use for us. In this world, I’m delivering code to an expert coder and I can assume that this coder can easily understand and modify my code if the user need differs a bit from what I expected.

Good software design has always depended on a good specification of user requirements. Now user requirements can change on the fly. My agent can modify the code to suit my particular use case.

We should think about software as having two parts: (1) an immutable part that is the contract about the core method and what it does. And (2) a modifiable part that the AI can adapt to different use cases.

There are lots of example of how this plays out. The simplest example is probably a GUI. It's easy for Claude to build an interface tailored to what I like. Why would I settle for a GUI designed by someone who doesn’t know my task and my tastes?

In computer vision, algorithms that are designed or trained for a specific case may be adaptable to other cases. As a trivial example, imagine a method that estimates the 3D pose of a person in an image but is not designed to process video. It’s easy for an AI to take this core method and build a method that works on video.

The mindset change is to deliver software into the “hands” of an expert AI coder that can understand and modify the code. This changes the contract between designer and user. The designer is now just providing a springboard that the user can exploit to finish the job.

fullText:
Great weekend read from Stanford on measuring AI agents as teammates.

(bookmark it)

If you build multi-agent systems or build with agent teams, this one is worth your time.

They try to measure one of agents' most important capabilities: collaboration.

They propose the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark, which has 240 tasks across 8 teamwork skills. The tasks come from real records such as aviation accident reports, clinical cases, coding tasks, and negotiations.

The best of 18 models scores 82.2/100. Every model loses 20 to 47 points once a teammate creates a problem.

Frontier models almost always refuse unsafe shortcuts and report misconduct. Holding a position under pressure is much harder for them.

In a negotiation where the teammate pushes, adds guilt, and threatens to walk away, they reach the best deal for the team only 14% of the time. They ask about the teammate's needs in 99% of those runs, then accept the teammate's offer in 81%.

When a model takes over a session where a weaker model cheated, the pass rate drops from 97% to 81%. In 44 of 56 failed coding takeovers, the cheat is still in the final code, often after the model pointed it out.

Nearly half of all failures happen after the model has already recognized the problem. Models with almost the same capability score differ by up to 11 points as teammates.

160 of the tasks are public with code and data. The other 80 are held out for evaluation.
